title: Paediatrics I: Neonatology, Growth and Nutrition
description: Newborn assessment and resuscitation, common neonatal problems, growth and development, infant feeding, malnutrition and immunisation.

topics.title: Newborn Assessment and Resuscitation
topics.summary: Apgar score, neonatal resuscitation, examination of the newborn, and thermal care.

notes.b: Most newborns need only drying, warmth and stimulation. The Apgar score (at 1 and 5 minutes) assesses heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability and colour (each 0–2; total 7–10 normal, 4–6 moderately depressed, 0–3 severely depressed); it describes condition but should not delay resuscitation. Neonatal resuscitation (Helping Babies Breathe / NLS): dry and stimulate; if not breathing, clear the airway if needed and start bag–mask ventilation with room air within the Golden Minute (40–60 breaths per minute); assess heart rate (< 100 bpm — continue ventilation, check chest rise; < 60 bpm despite effective ventilation — chest compressions 3:1 with ventilation, then adrenaline). Birth asphyxia (perinatal asphyxia) is a leading cause of neonatal death and of hypoxic–ischaemic encephalopathy (Sarnat staging) in Nigeria. Routine care: delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin, early breastfeeding, vitamin K, eye prophylaxis, chlorhexidine cord care, BCG, OPV0 and hepatitis B vaccines, and a full newborn examination (congenital anomalies, hips, spine, palate, red reflex, femoral pulses).

Newborns lose heat rapidly (evaporation, conduction, convection, radiation); hypothermia (< 36.5 °C) increases mortality — use the warm chain: warm delivery room, immediate drying, skin-to-skin, delayed bathing (at least 24 hours), caps and clothing, kangaroo mother care, and incubators or radiant warmers. Classification by gestation: preterm (< 37 weeks), term (37–41+6), post-term (≥ 42); by weight: low birth weight (< 2,500 g), very low (< 1,500 g), extremely low (< 1,000 g); by weight for gestation: small (SGA, < 10th centile — growth restriction), appropriate and large (LGA — maternal diabetes). The Ballard score estimates gestational age. Preterm infants face respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency — CPAP, surfactant), apnoea (caffeine), hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, infection, jaundice, necrotising enterocolitis, intraventricular haemorrhage and retinopathy of prematurity (screen those at risk; oxygen should be targeted).

topics.title: Common Neonatal Problems
topics.summary: Neonatal jaundice, sepsis, hypoglycaemia, tetanus and feeding problems.

notes.b: Neonatal jaundice is very common and a major cause of preventable brain damage in Nigeria (kernicterus — bilirubin encephalopathy, causing dyskinetic cerebral palsy, deafness and death). Physiological jaundice appears after 24 hours, peaks on days 3–5 and resolves by 2 weeks (term). Pathological jaundice: appears within 24 hours (always pathological — haemolysis: ABO or Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency — very common in Nigeria and worsened by exposure to naphthalene/mothballs, herbal remedies and menthol), rises rapidly, exceeds treatment thresholds, is prolonged (> 14 days term; > 21 days preterm — consider biliary atresia if stools are pale and urine dark, breast milk jaundice, hypothyroidism, infection), or conjugated. Assess serum bilirubin (or transcutaneous) against gestation- and age-specific charts; phototherapy (blue light converts bilirubin to water-soluble isomers; filtered sunlight phototherapy is being studied in Nigeria); exchange transfusion for very high levels or signs of encephalopathy. Biliary atresia requires Kasai portoenterostomy before 60 days.
k: Pale stools: biliary atresia — Kasai before 60 days

notes.b: Neonatal sepsis: early-onset (< 72 hours — maternal organisms: Group B streptococcus, E. coli, Klebsiella; risk factors: prolonged rupture of membranes, maternal fever, preterm birth) and late-onset (hospital or community — Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella, Gram-negatives; often multidrug-resistant in Nigerian NICUs). Signs are non-specific: poor feeding, lethargy, temperature instability, respiratory distress, apnoea, jaundice, convulsions, bulging fontanelle. Investigate (blood culture, FBC, CRP, lumbar puncture) and start antibiotics promptly (ampicillin plus gentamicin first-line; adjust to local resistance). Neonatal hypoglycaemia (glucose < 2.6 mmol/L; at-risk: preterm, SGA, infants of diabetic mothers, sick babies): feed or give IV 10% dextrose 2 mL/kg. Neonatal tetanus (unclean cord care, unimmunised mother; onset at 3–10 days with inability to suck, spasms, trismus) — prevented by maternal tetanus immunisation and clean delivery practices.
k: Neonatal tetanus: unclean cord, unimmunised mother

topics.title: Growth and Development
topics.summary: Growth monitoring, growth charts, developmental milestones and developmental delay.

notes.b: Growth is monitored with WHO growth standards: weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-length/height, head circumference and BMI-for-age, plotted over time (z-scores or centiles). Birth weight roughly doubles by 5 months and triples by 1 year; length increases by 50% in the first year; head circumference is about 35 cm at birth (rapid growth in infancy — microcephaly or macrocephaly/hydrocephalus warrant evaluation). Faltering growth (crossing centiles downwards) prompts assessment of feeding, illness (HIV, TB, malaria, chronic diarrhoea, heart and kidney disease) and psychosocial factors. Short stature: familial, constitutional delay, malnutrition, chronic disease, hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency and syndromes (Turner). Puberty: girls start with breast development (thelarche, 8–13 years), boys with testicular enlargement (9–14 years); precocious or delayed puberty need evaluation.
k: Birth weight ×2 by 5 months, ×3 by 1 year

notes.b: Development is assessed across domains: gross motor, fine motor/vision, speech/language/hearing, and social/emotional. Key milestones: social smile 6 weeks; head control 3–4 months; reaching and grasping 4–5 months; sitting without support 6–8 months; pincer grasp 9–10 months; stranger anxiety 8–9 months; standing and first words ~12 months; walking independently 12–15 months (red flag: not walking by 18 months); two-word phrases 2 years (red flag: no words by 18 months); drawing a circle 3 years. Limit ages (not the average age) trigger referral. Developmental delay may be global (cerebral palsy, intellectual disability, hypothyroidism, severe malnutrition, neonatal jaundice sequelae) or domain-specific (hearing loss causing speech delay; autism spectrum disorder — impaired social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviours). Regression (loss of skills) is always a red flag. Early stimulation, responsive caregiving and early intervention improve outcomes.
k: No words by 18 months: red flag

topics.title: Infant Feeding and Malnutrition
topics.summary: Breastfeeding, complementary feeding, acute and chronic malnutrition, and micronutrient deficiencies.

notes.b: WHO recommends early initiation of breastfeeding within 1 hour, exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months (no water, glucose water or herbal drinks — still commonly given in Nigeria), and continued breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond, with safe, adequate complementary foods from 6 months (thick pap/ogi enriched with protein such as fish, egg, legumes (e.g. beans, groundnut), fruit and vegetables; frequency increasing with age). Breast milk provides ideal nutrition, antibodies (secretory IgA), lactoferrin and protection against diarrhoea, pneumonia and obesity; benefits mothers (lactational amenorrhoea, reduced breast and ovarian cancer). Good attachment: mouth wide open, lower lip turned out, chin touching breast, more areola visible above than below. Mothers living with HIV on effective ART should breastfeed exclusively for 6 months and continue. Breastfeeding problems include sore nipples (poor attachment), engorgement, mastitis and perceived insufficient milk.

Nigeria has one of the highest burdens of child malnutrition (stunting about 35–40%, wasting about 7%; worst in the north-west and north-east). Severe acute malnutrition (SAM): weight-for-height < −3 SD, MUAC < 11.5 cm (6–59 months), or bilateral pitting oedema. Marasmus (severe wasting — 'old man' face, loose skin folds) and kwashiorkor (oedema, skin changes — flaky paint dermatosis, hair changes — sparse, pale; hepatomegaly, apathy; associated with inadequate protein and oxidative stress). Complicated SAM (poor appetite, medical complications) needs inpatient care following the WHO 10 steps: treat/prevent hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and dehydration (ReSoMal — cautious; avoid IV fluids unless shock), correct electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) and micronutrients (no iron initially), treat infection (antibiotics for all), start cautious feeding (F-75), catch-up growth (F-100 or RUTF), sensory stimulation and follow-up. Uncomplicated SAM with good appetite is treated as outpatients with RUTF (CMAM). Micronutrient deficiencies: vitamin A (xerophthalmia, night blindness — supplementation), iron (anaemia), iodine (goitre, cretinism), zinc (diarrhoea — zinc supplements), and rickets (vitamin D/calcium deficiency — bowed legs, rachitic rosary).

topics.title: Immunisation and Child Health Promotion
topics.summary: Vaccines and schedule, contraindications, cold chain, and well-child care.

notes.b: Nigeria's routine schedule: birth — BCG, OPV0, HepB0; 6, 10, 14 weeks — pentavalent (DTP-HepB-Hib), PCV, OPV, rotavirus (6 and 10 weeks), IPV (14 weeks); 6 months — vitamin A; 9 months — measles, yellow fever, meningococcal A conjugate (in the belt), IPV2 (fractional or full); 15 months — measles 2; HPV vaccine for girls 9–14 years; malaria vaccine (R21) in selected states from 5 months. Vaccine types: live attenuated (BCG, OPV, measles, yellow fever, rotavirus — avoid in severe immunosuppression, though most HIV-positive children should still receive measles and rotavirus), inactivated/subunit/conjugate (pentavalent, PCV, IPV, HepB, HPV), and toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria). True contraindications are few: anaphylaxis to a previous dose or component, and live vaccines in severe immunodeficiency and pregnancy. Minor illness, malnutrition, prematurity and antibiotic use are NOT contraindications (missed opportunities). BCG causes a scar at 2–6 weeks; a missing scar is not a reason to revaccinate routinely.
k: Live vaccines: caution in severe immunosuppression
Minor illness is not a contraindication

notes.b: Well-child visits combine growth monitoring, developmental surveillance, immunisation, vitamin A and deworming (albendazole from 12 months, every 6 months), counselling on feeding, hygiene, sleeping under insecticide-treated nets, home safety (burns from kerosene, poisoning, drowning, road safety) and early stimulation. The Road to Health card/child health booklet records growth and vaccines. Oral health (fluoride, limiting sugary drinks), vision and hearing screening, and newborn screening for sickle cell disease are increasingly emphasised. Adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) — mostly mild (fever, local pain); serious events (anaphylaxis, BCG lymphadenitis, vaccine-derived polio rarely) must be reported. Vaccine hesitancy (misinformation, religious and cultural beliefs, distrust — e.g. the 2003 Kano polio vaccine boycott) is addressed by engaging traditional and religious leaders, community mobilisers and clear communication.
